plain_text:
LONDONDERRY BUDGET COMMITTEE 
Meeting Minutes – November 17th, 2026 
Meeting Minutes prepared by Matt Tapley 
Moose Hill Council Chambers, 268B Mammoth Road, Londonderry, NH 03053 
1. Attendance 
Present: 
• Kate Burbidge (Chair)  
• Isaac Fernandez (Member at Large)  
• Nicole Dery (Vice-Chair)  
• Matt Tapley (Secretary)  
• Andria Hansen (Member at Large)  
• Rebecca Roe (Member at Large)  
• Jeff Penta (Member at Large) — arrived approximately 10 minutes late 
Absent: 
• Shawn Faber (Town Council Liaison)  
Town Staff and Guests: 
• Kim Bernard (Acting Town Manager and Police Chief)  
• Kirsten Hildonen (Administrative Services Director)  
• Justin Campo (Finance Director)  
• Sarah Jardim-Lee (Controller)  
• Drew Caron (Cable Director)  
• Donna Plant (Acting Library Director)  
• Nancy Hendricks (Library Trustees Chair)  
• Erica Laue (Library Trustees Secretary)  
• Azra Palo (Library Trustee)  
• Megan Donovan (Head of Circulation and Teen Services)  
• Doug Cole (Recreation Director)  
• Sherry Farrell (Town Clerk)  
• Dave Wholley (Public Works Director)  
• James Danis (Deputy Public Works Director)  
• Robert Kerry (Environmental Engineer)  
• Donna Limoli (Public Works Administrative Assistant)  
2. Call to Order 
Chair Kate Burbidge called the meeting to order at 6:30 PM, and the Committee recited 
the Pledge of Allegiance.
3. Public Comment 
Motions to open and close public comment were made and seconded and carried by 
voice vote. No one came forward to speak. 
4. New Committee Business 
The Committee reviewed proposed FY2028 budgets for Cable, Leach Library, 
Recreation, Town Clerk, Public Works solid waste and sewer, and Senior Affairs. 
Members discussed operating requests, default budgets, staffing and proposed warrant 
articles. 
4.1 Cable 
• The Cable Director presented a proposed budget of $316,441, a 6.08% increase. 
The department reported increased programming and production, a second 
podcasting room and sound booth, camera upgrades, and continued after-school, 
summer and high school programs. 
• The proposal increased equipment funding by approximately $9,500 to cover repairs 
and replacements without relying on emergency approvals. General expenses 
reflected reclassification of purchased services. Telephone and internet costs 
included service to the Town Common bandstand. The Director expected savings 
from changing custodial providers. Reduced training and travel reflected sending one 
employee, rather than two, to the annual industry trade show. Other reductions 
included unused subscriptions and part-time staffing funds. 
• Staff explained that Comcast franchise revenue, budgeted at approximately 
$500,000, exceeded the department's operating costs. The agreement runs through 
2030. Separate equipment funding supports larger purchases. Excess franchise 
revenue goes to the general fund and helps reduce the tax rate. Members asked 
about consolidating telephone, internet and custodial contracts. Staff believed most 
Comcast services were under the Town's umbrella but would need to verify the 
Cable Department's arrangements on school property. Custodial contracts are 
handled by building. 
4.2 Leach Library 
• Acting Library Director Donna Plant and Trustee Chair Nancy Hendricks reviewed 
the library's response to the burst pipe and approximately seven-and-a-half-month 
building closure. Services continued through a satellite location at the Police 
Department and programs at other community sites. During the closure, 750 patrons 
borrowed 14,779 items at consortium libraries, nearly 6,000 consortium items 
circulated through the satellite location, and digital circulation exceeded 33,000 
items.
• Plant reviewed the $51,000 reduction to the FY2027 library budget of $1,628,230. 
The trustees reduced salary-related allocations without eliminating positions, 
programming, collections, databases, periodicals, museum passes and supplies. 
Hoopla was being discontinued because its per-use pricing made costs difficult to 
predict. Staff reported spending just over $15,000 on Hoopla in FY2026 and 
explained that shared digital services offered lower costs per circulation. 
• The proposed FY2028 department budget increased approximately 1.88%. Wage 
increases for newly unionized staff would be addressed through a separate contract 
warrant article. Six new budget lines would distinguish consortium costs, electronic 
materials and programming by age group. The photocopier lease moved from 
maintenance to printing. The proposal restored $7,500 for legal services, increased 
maintenance from $25,000 to $35,000, and provided additional equipment, furniture 
and collection funding. Some collection funding would restore heavily requested 
genealogy and investment databases, while the remainder would address rising 
material costs. 
• The trustees planned five warrant articles: a bond for building project phase 2b, the 
union contract, a noncapital reserve fund initially funded with $20,000, a full-time 
executive assistant estimated at $122,050 annually, and a full-time library technician 
estimated at $131,287 annually including benefits. The executive assistant would 
support administration, communications and expanded services, including a possible 
passport acceptance program. The library technician would provide frontline support 
and allow the library to retain regular hours during the summer. 
• Members asked about part-time alternatives, service demand, potential passport 
revenue, legal expenses and equipment replacement. Staff said a part-time assistant 
would help but might limit the proposed new services. Passport processing could 
generate a $35 facility fee per application; Milford was cited as an established 
program generating up to $60,000 annually, with Londonderry's potential dependent 
on staffing and appointments. Plant said she would prioritize the executive assistant 
if only one position were funded. No position was approved at this meeting. 
• Trustees reported approximately $26,000 in union negotiation legal expenses from 
December 2025 through August 2026. Staff would need to follow up on other legal 
costs, some of which had been covered through the Town's legal budget. Staff 
clarified that the library's equipment was not included in the Cyber Services 
equipment detail discussed at the meeting. Trustees were working with Bob Slater 
on a comprehensive maintenance plan and had begun participating in capital 
improvement planning. 
• The library reported approximately 10,000 registered patrons and an authorized 
staffing complement of eight full-time and ten part-time positions, with three 
vacancies. Staff described a weekly staffing shortfall of approximately 45 hours even 
when fully staffed, affecting inventory, shelf reading and other work. Summer hours 
had been reduced by seven hours per week, selected using attendance patterns. 
Members encouraged measurable data to support staffing and service requests.
4.3 Recreation 
• Recreation Director Doug Cole presented an increase of just over $90,000, or 
25.62%, from an FY2027 budget of approximately $351,000. The proposal was 
approximately $70,000 above default. Major changes included seasonal 
maintenance staffing, utility costs, a needs assessment and facility improvements. 
• The proposal added 478 seasonal maintenance hours, bringing each of two positions 
to 800 hours, and increased pay to improve recruitment and retention. Utility 
estimates reflected prior underfunding and an anticipated 44% water rate increase. 
Portable toilet costs moved from supplies to management services, and background 
checks moved to Human Resources. Vehicle maintenance and equipment 
purchases decreased following replacement of the older van and prior equipment 
purchases. 
• Cole proposed an independent recreation needs assessment to guide priorities, 
resource allocation and future funding opportunities. He discussed potential 
university and hybrid approaches to collecting the data. Facility requests included 
$10,000 for the Funway playground pavilion cover and phased replacement of LAFA 
field dugouts, potentially supported by league contributions, sponsorships or grants. 
Members discussed the assessment's relationship to the Town master plan and the 
safety requirements for field maintenance and equipment operation. 
• Cole reported 358% participation growth over three years and approximately 18% 
growth in the current year. Program fees support a separate revolving fund that pays 
program costs and camp staff rather than the general fund. Staff cited FY2026 camp 
revenue of $107,465 and described how the revolving fund allowed additional 
counselors as enrollment increased. Facility rental policies and league agreements 
were being developed following adoption of the master fee schedule. 
• Cole requested restoration of the part-time assistant recreation director at 28 hours 
per week without benefits. The position was on the organizational chart but was not 
funded in the proposal. He estimated that adding programs two or three days per 
week could generate approximately $68,000 annually in additional gross revenue. 
The Chair suggested placing the position in the operating budget. Staff clarified that 
the additional seasonal maintenance hours were already included in the proposed 
budget. No funding action was taken. 
4.4 Town Clerk 
• The Town Clerk presented a request approximately 4.9%, or just under $30,000, 
above default. Principal drivers were employee cost-of-living adjustments, three 
major elections in FY2028, and higher printing, mailing and supply costs. The seven-
person office handles vehicle registrations, tax collection, vital records, dog licenses, 
elections and public records, and processes more than $100 million in annual 
revenue.
• Election costs included maintenance and service contracts for 18 poll pads and ten 
tabulators, as well as absentee ballot postage. The Clerk sought replacement of up 
to 50 aging voting booths and reported limited market options costing approximately 
$1,000 to $1,100 per unit. A phased purchase or trial of a few units remained 
possible. Members asked about tabulator life cycles and replacement planning; the 
Clerk estimated five to ten years and discussed potentially replacing equipment in 
stages. 
• Members also asked about digitization and historical records. The Clerk said 
digitization was ongoing, while older records in the vault remained undigitized. 
Preservation costs could reach approximately $5,000 per volume, and grant 
opportunities were discussed. 
4.5 Public Works 
• The Public Works Director, deputy director and environmental engineer presented 
the solid waste and sewer divisions, following earlier presentations on other Public 
Works functions. Staff announced that the seasonal drop-off center would close for 
the year on Saturday, November 21, and that household hazardous waste collection 
would take place that day from 8:30 AM to 12:30 PM at DPW, 120 High Range 
Road. 
• Solid waste staff reported an increase of approximately $288,000 from FY2027 and a 
proposal approximately $592 above default. Waste collection and recycling costs 
increased approximately 9.7% and 6.4%, respectively. Staff described growth in 
households served and trash tonnage, approximately 18,000 carts, and about 
13,500 weekly pickups. Cart replacement funding increased from $30,000 to $40,000 
because of aging and damaged carts. 
• Staff estimated combined curbside trash and recycling costs at $21.84 per residential 
unit per month. Projected disposal rates of $110.25 per ton for trash and $89 for 
recycling produced estimated savings of approximately $40,000 from recycling. Staff 
discussed home composting and other food waste diversion opportunities. 
• The drop-off center recorded nearly 8,000 paying visits in FY2026, in addition to 
visits for materials accepted without charge. The projected net operating cost 
increased approximately $63,000, reflecting usage growth and upcoming vendor 
bids. Staff said disposal fees had been unchanged since 1998 and were under 
review. Members discussed resident verification, cost recovery and the risk of illegal 
dumping. Staff had not developed a revised fee schedule and were not proposing a 
brush or yard waste charge at this stage. 
• The proposed sewer budget was approximately $5.346 million, funded entirely 
through the sewer enterprise fund. The roughly 29% reduction primarily reflected 
completion of most of the approximately $4.6 million Pillsbury Road pump station 
project, with about $743,000 remaining. Increases included approximately $1.1 
million for usage services, $304,000 for machinery and equipment, and $130,000 for 
management services. Drivers included Manchester treatment plant upgrades, 
additional Derry capacity, a sewer rate study and collection system capacity analysis.
• Staff reviewed maintenance of approximately 45 miles of sewer, more than 800 
manholes and six pump stations, with two additional stations anticipated. The system 
has an estimated replacement value exceeding $60 million. Responsibilities include 
regular inspections, industrial pretreatment compliance, development review and 
quarterly billing. The Director emphasized the environmental engineer's workload 
and 24-hour on-call responsibility, reiterated the request for an additional full-time 
truck driver, and identified a future need for another engineer. 
4.6 Senior Affairs 
• Finance Director Justin Campo presented Senior Affairs in the director's absence. 
Approximately $68,000 in potential building and equipment needs was outlined over 
the next five to seven years, including the roof, floors, parking lot, painting and 
appliances; HVAC and furnace quotes were still being obtained. These were future 
planning estimates rather than a single-year request. 
• The proposal removed CART transportation from the property-tax-supported 
operating budget because vehicle registration fees now support the service. Utilities 
and related building costs would move into Senior Affairs to show the full cost of the 
facility. Other proposed increases covered membership and attendance tracking, 
cleaning, pest control, service contracts and supplies. 
• Staff explained that program fees, memberships and rentals support a separate 
revolving fund. The fund had approximately $65,000 at the end of the prior fiscal year 
and a reported current balance of approximately $75,000. Annual gross receipts 
were estimated at $45,000 to $50,000, with program expenses paid from those 
receipts. Members asked about membership counts and revenue; a membership 
count was not available. The operating budget remains separately supported by 
taxation. 
5. Liaison Reports 
No separate liaison reports were recorded. 
6. Old Committee Business 
No separate old committee business was recorded. 
7. Other Business 
7.1 Department Follow Up and Budget Recommendations 
• The Chair asked members to email her by Monday, November 23, identifying 
departments they wished to hear from again on December 1 or December 8, or 
confirming that no return presentation was needed. Staff clarified that all 
departments had already been discussed, including Cemetery and General 
Government, and were available for follow-up as requested. Members raised 
questions about DPW equipment storage and the relationship between facilities and 
equipment life.
• Proposed warrant articles were available on the Town website. Staff recommended 
discussing them while the relevant department was present. A public hearing on the 
library bond was expected at a December Town Council meeting. Staff clarified that 
the part-time Recreation and Human Resources requests were in neither the 
operating proposal nor warrant articles, and that DPW equipment was not a warrant 
article. 
• The Committee discussed providing recommendations to the Town Council before 
and during its budget review. The Chair offered to consolidate member comments for 
a possible Council appearance. Staff described dedicated columns for Budget 
Committee recommendations by department and account. Members considered 
using the January 5 workshop to review recommendations, but deferred scheduling 
decisions to December 1. The December 1 meeting would take place at 6:30 PM 
even if no departments returned. 
7.2 Budget Questions and Information Sharing 
• Members were directed to email department questions to Justin Campo and copy the 
Chair. Staff and the Chair would coordinate responses and distribute information so 
members had equal access and departments did not receive duplicate requests. 
Staff also agreed to share budget-related Town Council questions and answers with 
the Committee. The discussion emphasized avoiding reply-all exchanges and 
sequential deliberations outside public meetings. 
7.3 School Budget Review 
• The Chair reported a 21.3% school health insurance cost increase, estimated to add 
approximately $3 million to the school budget, and said electronic budget books 
would be distributed. The next school budget presentation was confirmed for 
Tuesday, November 24, at 6:00 PM in the Londonderry High School cafeteria. Staff 
confirmed the school meetings shown on the schedule were at 6:00 PM. 
8. Approval of Minutes 
A motion to approve the November 10, 2026 minutes was made and seconded. The 
motion carried by voice vote, with an abstention recorded. 
9. Upcoming Meetings and Events 
Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at 6:00 PM: school budget presentation in the 
Londonderry High School cafeteria. No meeting was scheduled for Thursday, November 
19. 
Tuesday, December 1, 2026, at 6:30 PM: department follow-up as requested and 
discussion of the Committee's recommendation process and meeting schedule, 
including December 8.
10. Adjournment 
The Chair did not reopen public comment because no members of the public remained. 
A motion to adjourn was made and seconded and carried by voice vote. The Chair 
declared the meeting adjourned at 9:54 PM.
